cards.design_implication: If designing a chemoresistive sensor based on 2D heterostructures, the sensing mechanism should target the modulation of charge carrier concentration via surface adsorption of analytes.
does_not_establish: Whether this mechanism is universal for all 2D material combinations.
The exact magnitude of carrier concentration change for specific gases without experimental data.
cards.evidence_excerpt: Usually, the detected molecules are adsorbed onto the 2D material surface and act as electron donors or acceptors, thereby modifying the charge carrier concentration in the 2D material and, ultimately, its conductivity.
limitations: This description applies specifically to the chemoresistive sensing mechanism discussed in the context of gas sensors based on graphene/MoS2 heterostructures.
cards.statement: In van der Waals heterostructure gas sensors, gas molecules act as electron donors or acceptors upon adsorption, modifying the charge carrier concentration in the 2D material and its conductivity.

cards.design_implication: When selecting materials for sensor design, one must account for the zero-bandgap of pristine graphene affecting optoelectronic utility and potential environmental instability of transition metal dichalcogenides.
does_not_establish: Specific quantitative limits of stability for particular TMDs.
The exact performance gains from overcoming these drawbacks in all configurations.
cards.evidence_excerpt: By combining diferent 2D materials to form van der Waals heterostructures (VDWHs) it is possible to overcome the drawback of individual materials (such as inertness and zero-bandgap of pristine graphene and less environmental stability of transition metal dichalcogenides).
limitations: This claim identifies general drawbacks of individual materials that heterostructures aim to address.
cards.statement: Pristine graphene has a zero-bandgap, which is a drawback for optoelectronic applications, and transition metal dichalcogenides can suffer from less environmental stability.

cards.design_implication: Experimental designs must distinguish between calculating LOD (based on background noise standard deviation and slope) and sensitivity (response vs concentration), as they represent different performance metrics.
does_not_establish: A single universal threshold for what constitutes a 'good' LOD or sensitivity value.
Specific experimental protocols for reducing noise to approach the theoretical LOD.
cards.evidence_excerpt: It is also important to diferentiate LOD and sensitivity. LOD indi cates the theoretical minimum detectable concentration/amount owing to the background noise, which can be calculated by Equation (1).<sup>[34]</sup> Nevertheless, the value determined experimentally is typically much higher than the efective LOD due to the noise. The sensitivity is defined as the response normalized by the concentration of the analyte,
limitations: The text notes that experimentally determined LOD values are typically higher than the theoretical effective LOD due to noise.
cards.statement: Limit of detection (LOD) is theoretically defined by the minimum detectable concentration/amount owing to background noise, while sensitivity is the response normalized by the concentration of the analyte.
